title: Nasdaq Jumps 1.1 Percent as Chip and AI Stocks Rebound From Their Worst Week Since June
excerpt: The semiconductor index snapped an eight-day losing streak — its longest since 2008 — as Goldman and Morgan Stanley calls pulled bargain hunters back into the AI trade.
body:
• The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.11 percent to 26,430.89 on Monday and the S&P 500 gained 0.42 percent to 7,691.07, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.06 percent to 51,970.20.
  • The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index jumped 3.7 percent, snapping an eight-day losing streak — its longest since October 2008 — after falling about 15.7 percent during the slide.
  • Micron rose 5.3 percent, Broadcom 3.2 percent and Amazon 5.2 percent as bargain hunters returned to the AI trade a week after the S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their biggest weekly drops since late June.
  • Earnings now decide whether the bounce holds: SpaceX reports Tuesday, with Meta Platforms and Tesla due Wednesday.

Wall Street's AI trade found its footing on Monday. Chipmakers and data-centre stocks led a broad rebound as investors bought last week's selloff, which had been driven by a question the market has deferred for months: how the enormous cost of building AI infrastructure gets financed, and whether the returns arrive before the patience runs out.

Chips lead the snapback

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 3.7 percent, ending an eight-day losing streak that was its longest run of declines since October 2008. Micron jumped 5.3 percent and Broadcom climbed 3.2 percent, according to Reuters. CoreWeave — at the centre of last week's rout after its shares plunged more than 25 percent on concern over a $50 billion debt load — gained 3.1 percent after Goldman Sachs upgraded the company to "buy" from "neutral," arguing the selloff had created an opening. AI infrastructure peers Nebius and Iren rose 4.7 percent and 6.5 percent respectively, and Amazon climbed 5.2 percent after Morgan Stanley named it a "top pick."

"Nothing changed between Friday's close and this morning's open, other than nothing bad happened over the weekend, and sentiment had gotten so negative that we were oversold to the point where a bounce was due."

— Michael James, Managing Director at Rosenblatt Securities

The worry has not gone away

One session of bargain hunting does not answer the financing question. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq had just posted their biggest weekly declines since late June, on concern that higher interest rates could curb investment in AI infrastructure — pressure that fell hardest on data-centre operators carrying heavy debt. The bull market recently marked its fourth anniversary, and the companies underpinning it are the same ones now being asked to show that AI spending converts into revenue.

Earnings week is the real test

The calendar is unforgiving. SpaceX reports on Tuesday, and Meta Platforms and Tesla follow on Wednesday, with Netflix, General Motors and GE Aerospace also reporting this week. "What investors really need is stronger monetization, proof that the revenues generated with AI can catch up with the spending on AI tools," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote. Monday's close — the Nasdaq up 290.85 points and the S&P 500 ahead 32.48, per preliminary data reported by Reuters — buys the trade a hearing. The earnings calls will deliver the verdict.
